transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2028-05-04 14:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes

Attendees:
- Sofia Patel (Redwood)
- Marcus Li (Redwood, Solutions Engineer)
- Lena Moreau (Astrolabe, Head of Cloud)
- Owen Reyes (Astrolabe, Network Eng)
- Priya Nair (Astrolabe, Security)

Auto-generated summary (brief):
Astrolabe is evaluating Redwood private deployment behind their VPC with strict EU-only data residency, HSM-backed KMS integration, and no public egress IPs. Primary ask: architecture options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink vs Transit), cert/mTLS options, static egress, and cross-account identity for S3/ECR access. They are leaning toward Dedicated/Private but need network diagrams and compliance docs before procurement.

Topics covered:
- connectivity options: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, Transit Gateway
- private endpoints, interface vs gateway endpoints (S3/ECR)
- region constraints and EU-only deployment
- KMS/HSM integration and key management for inference logs
- egress/IP curation, NLB/static IP and firewall chaining
- cross-account roles and IAM for S3/ECR pulls
- performance tradeoffs: latency vs batching/costs

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Patel (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call and then we'll dive into the network constraints. Marcus and I will cover the architectural options, and then leave time for Priya for any security specifics.
[00:18] Lena Moreau (Astrolabe): Hi, yeah thanks. We're tight on time so appreciate this. High level: data must stay in EU, prefer EU-West-1 and EU-North-1 for DR. We have a mix of AWS accounts and a central transit account.
[00:35] Marcus Li (Redwood SE): Cool. So three broad patterns we usually see — VPC peering cross-account, AWS PrivateLink/Interface endpoints, or Transit Gateway with a private endpoint. Each has tradeoffs on IP space and route complexity.
[00:50] Owen Reyes (Astrolabe): Can you explain the egress story? We can't have dynamic public IPs. Our security team needs whitelisted static addresses for upstream providers.
[01:05] Marcus Li: Right. For static egress we typically front Redwood Private with an NLB in the customer's VPC or use a managed egress NAT with fixed Elastic IPs. Another pattern is to use a dedicated NAT in a small egress account and then route through that.
[01:22] Priya Nair (Astrolabe): And for S3/ECR pulls — do you need internet access or can you use gateway endpoints? We want to avoid any internet path.
[01:34] Sofia: You can absolutely use gateway endpoints for S3 and interface endpoints for ECR; we support pulling images via cross-account roles when VPC endpoints are present. We do need a little setup for ECR auth — usually a role we assume from the Redwood runtime account.
[01:50] Owen: Ok, so anything about IP address collision? We run fairly small subnets, worried about peering conflicting CIDRs.
[02:03] Marcus: Yeah — peering requires non-overlapping CIDRs. If there's overlap, PrivateLink or Transit GW with NAT and proxying can work. We can also recommend transitive NAT patterns or using a small proxy fleet in a neutral account.
[02:20] Lena: We're also evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted — cost/throughput tradeoffs. Our throughput is heavy real-time inference, lots of small requests. Cold starts are painful.
[02:33] Sofia: For high throughput and low latency you might prefer Dedicated or Private with reserved capacity. Redwood Dedicated gives predictable units and you can colocate in the same region; Private lets you control the networking and keys.
[02:48] Owen: How do you handle KV cache and sessions? We saw a note about "KV cash" in an earlier doc — that's a typo, but we want to make sure cache keys aren't leaked.
[02:58] Marcus: Sorry the transcript said KV cash — yes KV cache. We keep KV cache local to the runtime and it's not persisted to customer buckets unless you opt into log export.
[03:12] Priya: Important: HSM-backed keys for model artifacts and logs, and we need to audit all key usage. Does Redwood integrate with customer KMS or HSM?
[03:24] Sofia: Yes — we support customer-managed KMS keys and many customers use CloudHSM-backed KMS keys. For Private deployments, the control plane can be configured to use the customer's KMS via cross-account grants. We'll share our KMS integration doc.
[03:38] Lena: About the control plane — do we have to open any public endpoints to allow the Redwood control plane to talk to the private runtime?
[03:48] Marcus: There's a couple of patterns. For fully air-gapped on-prem you'd run the control plane locally. For VPC Private deployment we typically have a small outbound-only tunnel/backchannel from the runtime to the Redwood control plane — that's egress-only TLS on port 443 to a pinned endpoint. If your policy forbids any egress you can host the control plane in your network.
[04:12] Owen: What about DNS and split-horizon? Can we host private DNS entries so the runtime resolves internal services only?
[04:21] Marcus: Yes, you can configure split-horizon DNS. When using PrivateLink we create internal private DNS names. With peering you can use the VPC resolver rules pointing to your Route53 inbound endpoints.
[04:35] Priya: We need mTLS for the runtime -> S3 and to Redwood telemetry endpoints. Does Redwood support client certs?
[04:45] Sofia: We support mTLS for control plane connections and mutual TLS to any customer endpoints in Private. For S3 we rely on signed requests via the assumed role; for telemetry you can route to a customer collector with mTLS.
[04:58] Lena: You mentioned cross-account IAM for ECR. Walk that through quickly.
[05:05] Marcus: We normally create a deployment role in the customer's account that Redwood assumes to pull images and for S3 access. The role has a trust policy limited to Redwood's runtime account. With PrivateLink and endpoint policies you can restrict it further.
[05:20] Owen: Are there ports or protocols we need to open inbound to our VPC?
[05:25] Sofia: For interface endpoints you need TCP 443 to the interface endpoint. If you're peering, then the runtime lives in your VPC space so you'd control whatever ports the runtime needs — usually 443 and some health-check ports between subnets.
[05:40] Priya: Audit logs — who holds them? We need to ensure logs are written to our S3 with encryption and retention locked.
[05:50] Marcus: In Private, logs can be written directly to your S3 bucket encrypted with your KMS. You can also stream logs to your SIEM via VPC egress.
[05:59] Lena: Any compliance docs we can see? SOC2, ISO, pen test reports?
[06:05] Sofia: Yes, we'll send SOC2 type II and our pen test summary as part of the package. Also a one-pager on our private deployment architecture.
[06:12] Marcus: Quick note: if you want region gating (EU only), we'll restrict available runtime regions and provide a region-tagged model set — it's part of the placement policy.
[06:25] Owen: About throughput — if we do batching to save cost does that increase latency beyond acceptable? Our SLA is sub-200ms for small prompts.
[06:35] Marcus: Batching can add tail latency. For low-latency SLAs you can configure tiny batch windows and use dedicated capacity with reserved concurrency. We'll show measured profiles for sequence lengths similar to yours.
[06:50] Priya: What about software supply chain — container signing and image provenance?
[06:55] Sofia: Redwood supports signed images (notarization) and we can require signed images in the deployment pipeline. We'll include our image signing docs.
[07:05] Lena: Ok, can you sketch two options briefly — (A) Transit GW approach with central egress and (B) VPC peering to runtime subnets?
[07:15] Marcus: Sure. Option A: Transit GW in your central account, route to a dedicated subnet hosting Redwood runtime via private link into a neutral account. Pros: easier CIDR reuse, single egress, easier auditing. Cons: more complex routing, extra hop. Option B: Cross-account VPC peering directly to runtime subnets. Pros: simpler path, lower hop count. Cons: requires non-overlapping CIDRs and more bilateral setup.
[07:45] Owen: Which supports static egress best?
[07:48] Marcus: Both can. With Transit GW you centralize EIPs. With peering you front the runtime with a NAT/ELB in your account with EIPs. The choice depends on your infra team preferences.
[08:00] Priya: We also have a mandated firewall appliance that inspects TLS. How do we do TLS inspection without exposing keys?
[08:10] Sofia: If you must decrypt at the firewall, you need the firewall to have the certs — that changes threat model. Alternative: use a telemetry proxy that forwards metadata while keeping payloads encrypted, or run the firewall in a pass-through mode and rely on egress allowlists. We can review options with your SecOps.
[08:30] Lena: On latency numbers — what's typical from EU-West to EU-West with dedicated?
[08:36] Marcus: Median token latency in our benchmarks for a 512 sequence on a dedicated worker is ~30-50ms per token under steady state — but depends on model and GPU. We'll share benchmarks for the models you listed.
[08:51] Owen: We are also concerned about rolling updates — can you do canary deploys and automatic fallback to a smaller model if something regresses?
[08:59] Sofia: Yes — Redwood supports canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback policies by model variant. Those are configurable in the console and we can restrict who can trigger them via RBAC.
[09:13] Priya: RBAC — SSO integrations? We use SAML/Okta.
[09:18] Marcus: We integrate with SAML, OIDC and support SCIM provisioning for user sync. For Private we can also integrate with your IdP via an enterprise connector.
[09:28] (short pause, background paper rustling)
[09:33] Owen: Quick question on costs — if we go Private, are we billed for egress separately?
[09:39] Sofia: For Private deployments, egress to customer services is typically on the customer's networking. Redwood charges for reserved capacity and support; egress is the customer's cloud egress. We'll include cost examples with bandwidth assumptions.
[09:52] Lena: Ok, can we get a sample network diagram and an exact checklist of endpoint rules you need?
[09:58] Marcus: Absolutely. We'll produce a diagram and a checklist showing required route targets, endpoint policies, and sample IAM trust policies.
[10:10] Sofia: One operational note — we recommend a short pilot: small cluster in EU-West with a limited model set for 2-3 weeks to run perf and compliance checks. After pilot, scale to DR region.
[10:24] Priya: That works. We'll need to review log retention settings and retention lock on S3.
[10:31] Marcus: We can set write-once buckets or retention via lifecycle rules; you own the S3 policies. We'll document recommended settings.
[10:40] Owen: Anything special for EKS-based infra? We run most services in EKS and would like Redwood runtime to access internal services like feature store over private endpoints.
[10:50] Marcus: You can use interface endpoints for internal services or peering — runtime inside your VPC can call internal feature store endpoints. We'll show a sample service mesh pattern.
[11:02] Lena: Let's talk timeline — procurement wants something in place by end of Q3. Security needs the docs by mid-May to start review.
[11:10] Sofia: Timeline sounds feasible. We'll aim to deliver security docs and diagrams by May 7, network diagram and estimate by May 10, and then set a pilot kickoff the week of May 20 if that lines up.
[11:25] (brief cross talk)
[11:30] Owen: Are there any IP allowlist requirements on your side? For the control plane callbacks?
[11:36] Marcus: We publish a small set of IP ranges for control plane egress; for Private you can pin to our egress endpoints or host the control plane locally. We'll share exact ranges in the checklist.
[11:50] Priya: Final note: will need a meeting with our SecOps and NetOps to go through deep packet inspection, cert management, and KMS grants. Can we schedule that?
[11:58] Sofia: Yes — we'll set that up. Marcus, can you lead the deep dive?
[12:03] Marcus: Happy to.
[12:07] Sofia: Ok let's do recap and next steps.
[12:10] (recap)
[12:12] Sofia: Next steps: we'll send SOC2/pen test + KMS integration doc, Marcus will send network diagram and checklist, Owen to provide CIDRs and egress IPs. We'll schedule SecOps deep dive.
[12:25] Lena: Thanks — that's great.
[12:28] Meeting end.
